newsitem.title: FINLAND: Russia promises tough line on NATO at summit.
newsitem.headline: Russia promises tough line on NATO at summit.

text.p: Russia promised a tough summit fight over NATO enlargement on Thursday, as President Boris Yeltsin's spokesman said the Kremlin chief would defend Moscow's interests "like never before" at the meeting.

With U.S. President Bill Clinton on his way to the Finnish capital, Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said it was possible to achieve results from the two-day summit which starts with a dinner later on Thursday.
But Yastrzhembsky, who said on Wednesday NATO enlargement would be the West's biggest mistake since the end of the Cold War, signalled Yeltsin was not in the mood for compromise on that issue.
"The president is ready to defend Russia's national interests firmly like never before," he told reporters.
Russia says NATO's plans to take in several former Soviet bloc states will threaten its security, undermine Yeltsin, create new divisions in Europe and represent a breach of trust.

Clinton is seeking to reassure Moscow that NATO enlargement presents no threat, while U.S. officials are hoping to shift the summit focus onto less contentious issues where progress is more likely, such as Russia's economic reforms.
Both sides say there is no intention of reaching a formal agreement on NATO at the Helsinki summit, the first time Clinton and Yeltsin have met in almost a year.

Yastrzhembsky said the aim was "to reach the highest level of mutual understanding, to understand better the concerns...of Russia and to understand better the reasons of the American decision on NATO expansion".
Nevertheless, the tough Russian line raises the prospect of serious public disagreement at the summit, despite the usual careful planning and preparation on both sides.

Washington has said it will not be deterred from NATO enlargement. An alliance summit in July is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to start membership talks. The new members would not join until 1999.
Before leaving Washington, Clinton said NATO enlargement was a top priority and that he wanted a "robust partnership" with Moscow to run in parallel.

"We are adapting NATO to take on new missions, enlarging NATO to take in new members, strengthening NATO's partnership with non-members and seeking to build a robust partnership between NATO and Russia," he said.

Yeltsin, on fighting form after months of illness and last year's heart surgery, has to keep a wary eye on his communist and nationalist critics at home and must be seen to fight Russia's corner in Helsinki.
His opponents are planning a strident anti-Western debate on NATO for Thursday in the Russian parliament, the Duma.
Clinton, temporarily confined to a wheelchair after a freak accident last week, was due to arrive in Helsinki at around 1000 GMT. Yeltsin arrives around three hours later.
The main talks take place on Friday in a modern, airy villa overlooking the Baltic, the official residence of Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari.
The U.S. president had agreed to move the summit from Washington to Helsinki because of Yeltsin's health problems, but now finds himself the invalid and on the defensive over NATO.
Washington and Moscow have enjoyed increasingly warm relations since the end of the Cold War but a chilly tone has crept into preparations for the Helsinki summit as the two nations argue about NATO.
While NATO enlargement tops the summit agenda, Moscow and Washington also plan to discuss problems in arms control and Russia's troubled transition to a market economy.

There is likely to be more Western help on offer to support Russia as it tackles organised crime and economic reforms, particularly since Yeltsin has pleased Washington by bringing young reformers into a new-look cabinet this week.
